## Finding a starting point {#fv2-proof-tips .fv-lesson .proof-lesson }

```{=html}
<div class="proof-basis">
<div><h3>In a plane</h3><p><strong>Two non-parallel vectors</strong></p><span data-math="\alpha\underset{\sim}{a}+\beta\underset{\sim}{b}"></span></div>
<div><h3>In 3D space</h3><p><strong>Three non-coplanar vectors</strong></p><span data-math="\alpha\underset{\sim}{a}+\beta\underset{\sim}{b}+\gamma\underset{\sim}{c}"></span></div>
</div>
<p><strong>Express every required vector using the same chosen vectors.</strong></p>
<ol class="proof-tips proof-tips-short"><li>Draw and label a diagram.</li><li>Check the direction of each vector.</li><li>Rewrite the required-to-prove statement (RTP) in vector notation.</li><li>Recall the geometric properties of the dot product.</li></ol>
```

<div class="booklet-cue">Booklet §2.2 · p. 13 · teacher’s proof tips</div>

::: {.notes}
Choose a fixed pair of non-parallel vectors for a plane: every vector in that plane is αa+βb. Choose three non-coplanar vectors for three-dimensional space: every vector is αa+βb+γc. Pairwise non-parallel is insufficient in 3D because all three might still lie in one plane. If a spatial problem is planar, two spanning vectors suffice. Choosing vectors from a common vertex often simplifies paths; the three edges from A in the triangular pyramid in Example 2.7 provide the spatial version. AB=−BA; head-minus-tail for position vectors. Establish the conditions you need rather than assuming the required conclusion. The chosen vectors need not be perpendicular or unit length.
:::
